Cinema · The Economist data, revisited

The Most-Referenced Film of 1980 Was Not Nominated

For 89 years, Best Picture has crowned the films the Academy thinks will last. The films audiences actually quote, parody and remake are increasingly chosen by it not to receive Best Picture.

In 1980, the most-referenced film of the year — by a factor of 18.6 — was The Empire Strikes Back. The Academy gave Best Picture to Ordinary People. The same year-#1 film, never even nominated, repeats again and again: Psycho (1960), 2001: A Space Odyssey (1968), The Terminator (1984), Back to the Future (1985), Jurassic Park (1993), The Matrix (1999), Pulp Fiction lost to Forrest Gump, Goodfellas lost to Dances with Wolves.

Of the 89 years from 1928 to 2016, the most-referenced film was not nominated for Best Picture in 52 of them — 58.4% of all years. Star Wars, Empire, Psycho, Frankenstein, Snow White, 2001, King Kong: the Academy did not consider any of them the year's best.

58.4% of years from 1928 to 2016, the most-referenced film was not even nominated for Best Picture

How a Reference Is Counted

Influence here is operationalized as IMDb "movie connections" — every time a later film, TV show, video game or music video quotes, parodies, homages or references the original. When Niles in Frasier says "Of all the coffee joints in all the towns in all the world…", that is one connection added to Casablanca. The Psycho strings in any horror comedy are connections to Psycho. The data is crowdsourced from millions of viewers.

"Of all the gin joints in all the towns in all the world, she walks into mine." Casablanca · 1942
one connection
"Of all the coffee joints in all the towns in all the world…" Niles in Frasier · 1990s
Casablanca has 1,454 connections like this. (Tap to highlight.)

The Economist assembled the data in early 2019 from a frozen IMDb snapshot taken at the end of 2017. They counted 28,763 films, computed each film's share of references among films released in the same year, and tagged Best Picture nominees and winners. We use the same numbers here, capped at 2016 releases as they did.

The obvious caveat is the recency problem: an older film has had more decades to accrue references, so we do not compare counts directly across years. Within a single year, every film is competing on the same clock — and that is the comparison the Academy itself is making when it picks Best Picture.

The Academy's Hit Rate Is Collapsing

The clearest test of the Academy's instinct is whether the winner is the year-#1 most-referenced film. Out of 89 winners, 14 — just 15.7% — were also #1 in their own year. The Academy is right less than one year in six.

The decade-by-decade trend is starker. In the 1960s and 1970s, 30% of winners were the year-#1 film. In the 1980s the rate fell to zero. It bounced back to 20% in the 1990s — then collapsed again. Across all seven Best Picture awards from 2010 to 2016, the year-#1 film was never the winner. Not once.

The mean year-rank of Best Picture winners follows the same curve: 3.5 in the 1970s, 14.0 in the 1980s, 11.6 in the 2010s. The Academy's eye for the era-defining film, sharpest in the New Hollywood years, has not recovered.

Best Picture Winners, By Decade
Bars: percentage of winners that were the most-referenced film of their year. Line: mean year-rank of winners (lower is better).
Source: The Economist / IMDb. Best Picture winners 1928–2016.

Best Picture, Year by Year

The path of every Best Picture winner through the rankings is a reverse trajectory. Casablanca (1943) captured 48.7% of all references for its year. The Godfather (1972) took 33.7%. Titanic (1997) took 17.2%. Spotlight (2015) — the most recent winner before our cutoff — took 0.78%. Moonlight (2016) took 1.08%.

The most recent winner above 10% was Titanic. The most recent winner above 5% was 2003's Lord of the Rings: The Return of the King. The current decade hovers between 1% and 2.5%.

Every Best Picture Winner, 1928–2016
Each dot is one Best Picture winner. Y-axis: share of all references in that year. Color: year-rank tier. Hover any dot for film, year, share and rank.
Source: The Economist / IMDb. 89 winners.

Set the winners aside and rebuild the record from the films that audiences actually reference. The most-referenced film of each year is a parallel canon: Frankenstein (1931), King Kong (1933), Snow White (1937), The Wizard of Oz (1939), Citizen Kane (1941), Vertigo (1958), Psycho (1960), 2001 (1968), The Godfather (1972), Jaws (1975), Star Wars (1977), Pulp Fiction (1994), Titanic (1997), The Matrix (1999). Sixteen of these are not Best Picture winners. Many were never nominated.

The Films the Academy Chooses Now

Twenty-two Best Picture winners — almost a quarter — finished outside the top 10 most-referenced films of their own year. The two most extreme: Cavalcade (1933, ranked 37th in its year) and The Last Emperor (1987, ranked 36th). In the 2010s, Spotlight ranked 25th and Moonlight 15th. Argo finished 11th. Only Birdman (6th) cracked the top 10 for the entire decade.

There is a pattern in what the Academy chooses now: intimate, sober dramas. Spotlight, Moonlight, The Artist, Birdman, 12 Years a Slave. These are reasonable films. But they generate few visual or verbal hooks for the wider culture to grab. Genre cinema — sci-fi, horror, action — is parody-rich, quote-rich, image-rich. The Academy votes against it almost reflexively.

The Cinema-Shaped Hole Is Smaller, Too

One reading of the decline is that audiences and creators are simply more spread out. The single most-referenced film of each year used to dominate. In the 1970s the year-#1 captured 22.6% of all references on average. In the 2000s it fell to 7.2%. In the 2010s, just 5.7% — a 4x drop from the 1970s peak. Even Star Wars: The Force Awakens, the most-referenced film of 2015, took only 9.0% of that year's references.

So the Academy's failure is not just relative — the cinema-shaped hole in the culture is bigger than it used to be. But the Academy is failing within that smaller hole. When The Force Awakens captured 9% and Spotlight captured 0.78%, the Academy chose a film that was 11 times less referenced than the year's leader.

Concentration of Cinematic Influence, By Decade
Mean share of all annual references captured by each year's #1 film. The single dominant film matters less than it used to.
Source: The Economist / IMDb.

What Is Left of the Canon

The Oscars used to function as a canon-maker. Winners got re-released, taught in film schools, shelved in the front of video stores. Best Picture viewership peaked at 55 million in 1998 — Titanic's year — and has been falling ever since. By 2018 it was 26.5 million, less than half.

None of this means the Academy is wrong about the films it does pick. Moonlight and Spotlight are good films. The point is narrower: the Academy used to be a reliable predictor of what the world would still talk about. It is not, anymore. The films we still quote, parody, and remake are increasingly chosen by the Academy not to receive Best Picture.

On the night a Best Picture winner is announced, the safest bet is that fewer people will reference it twenty years from now than will reference at least three other films released in the same year. That has been true, on average, for every decade since the 1980s. It will likely be true again next year.
